findings.claim: `Object.assign(this, cause)` in the constructor can clobber intrinsic Error fields such as `stack`, `name`, and `message`
findings.rationale: The source object is arbitrary unknown data. If it carries a `stack` or `name` key (common when serializing errors across a boundary, e.g. a plain object reconstructed from JSON), the freshly captured stack trace and the `Error`/`UnknownCauseError` name are silently overwritten, which degrades debuggability and can confuse downstream `err.name === '...'` checks. Previously the same assign happened at the call site, but doing it after `super()` here still means the message computed by `getMessage` can be replaced by a non-string `message` value. Medium confidence this matters in practice, but it is a real behavior hazard worth guarding (e.g. assigning only own enumerable keys that aren't `stack`/`name`).

findings.claim: `getMessage` turns an explicitly-`undefined` (or symbol/exotic) `message` property into a bogus string
findings.rationale: `'message' in cause` is true for `{ message: undefined }`, so `String(cause.message)` yields the literal string `"undefined"` as the error message instead of falling back to the empty default. Similarly `String()` on a symbol-valued message throws only for implicit conversion (String() is safe there), but an object with a null prototype or a throwing `toString`/getter will throw inside the constructor, turning a best-effort error-wrapping path into a thrown exception. High confidence on the `undefined` case; moderate on the throwing-`toString` case. Suggest `typeof cause.message === 'string' ? cause.message : undefined`.

findings.claim: Constructor now requires an argument — any existing `new UnknownCauseError()` call site must be updated
findings.rationale: The class previously had an implicit zero-arg constructor and the surrounding code presumably did `const err = new UnknownCauseError(); Object.assign(err, cause);`. The diff does not show the `getCauseFromUnknown` body being updated. If the old call site remains, it will fail to compile, or (if updated) may now perform `Object.assign` twice redundantly. Worth verifying the rest of the function was updated in the same change.
